name: Automate the Boring Stuff with Python, 3rd edition
author: Al Sweigart
note: Sections and key points for chapters 2-8 and 10 come from our checked outlines; other chapters are titles only.

items.heading: Boolean values
objectives: There are only two Boolean values, True and False, capitalized; lowercase true and false aren't valid (NameError)
True and False are keywords, so they can't be used as variable names (SyntaxError)
They aren't strings: True is different from 'True'
Boolean values can be stored in variables and used in expressions

items.heading: Comparison operators
objectives: The six comparison operators ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= each evaluate to True or False
== and != work with values of any type; <, >, <=, >= are meant for integers and floats
A number never equals a string, even one with the same digits, while an integer equals a float with the same value
== compares and = assigns; mixing them up is a classic mistake

items.heading: Boolean operators: and, or, not
objectives: and is True only when both sides are True; or is True when at least one side is; not flips one value (the truth table for each)
Comparisons can be combined with Boolean operators: each comparison gives a Boolean that the operator then works on
Order of operations: math and comparison operators first, then not, then and, then or
Boolean operators can be stacked, such as applying not more than once

items.heading: Conditions and blocks of code
objectives: A condition is an expression that evaluates to True or False and decides what a flow control statement does
Block rules: a block begins where indentation increases, can contain other blocks (nesting), and ends where indentation goes back to an enclosing level
Program execution normally runs top to bottom; flow control statements make it skip or jump
Flowcharts show branching: diamonds for decisions, rectangles for steps

items.heading: The if statement
objectives: Form: the if keyword, a condition, a colon, then an indented block (the clause)
The clause runs only when the condition is True; otherwise it's skipped
Every flow control statement ends with a colon followed by an indented block

items.heading: The else statement
objectives: else is optional, comes right after an if (or elif) clause, and has no condition
Its clause runs only when the condition before it was False, so exactly one of if and else runs

items.heading: The elif statement, and why the order of elif branches matters
objectives: elif gives another condition, checked only when every earlier condition in the chain was False
At most one clause in an if/elif chain runs: the first one whose condition is True
Order matters: a broad condition placed before a narrower one inside it makes the narrower one unreachable
Ending the chain with else guarantees exactly one clause runs

items.heading: Short example programs that combine if, else and elif
objectives: Separate if statements are each checked on their own, so several can run, unlike one if/elif chain
Flipping a Boolean variable with not
Accepting several possible inputs with or needs a full comparison on each side of or, not a bare value on the right
Converting input with float() and str() to do math with it
A variable that's assigned only in some branches doesn't exist when none of them ran, causing a NameError

items.heading: while loops
objectives: A while clause repeats as long as its condition is True; the condition is checked before each pass
At the end of the clause, execution jumps back to the condition, unlike an if
The loop variable needs a value before the loop so the condition can be checked the first time
A condition that never becomes False makes an infinite loop; Ctrl-C stops a stuck program

items.heading: break statements
objectives: break leaves the loop immediately
The while True: ... break pattern loops forever and exits from inside
break only works inside loops

items.heading: continue statements
objectives: continue jumps back to the start of the loop and checks the condition again
It skips the rest of one pass
continue only works inside loops

items.heading: for loops and the range() function
objectives: for i in range(5): runs its block 5 times, with i from 0 to 4
range(n) goes up to, but doesn't include, n
for loops suit a known number of repetitions; while loops suit repeating until something changes

items.heading: break and continue inside for loops
objectives: break and continue work in for loops the same way as in while loops
In a for loop, continue moves on to the next value of the loop variable

items.heading: Writing a for loop as an equivalent while loop
objectives: A for i in range(5) loop can be written as a while loop with a counter set before it and increased at the end of each pass
The for version is shorter because it manages the counter for you

items.heading: range() with start, stop and step arguments
objectives: range(start, stop) starts at start and stops just before stop
A third argument is the step between the numbers
A negative step counts down
When left out, the start defaults to 0 and the step to 1

items.heading: Importing modules from the standard library
objectives: An import statement makes a module's functions available, called with the module's name and a dot
Several modules can be imported in one statement, separated by commas
from module import * drops the module name, but full names are more readable
Don't name your own file after a standard module, or Python imports yours instead

items.heading: Ending a program early with sys.exit()
objectives: A program ends after its last line; sys.exit() ends it early
sys has to be imported first

items.heading: Short complete programs: a number guessing game and rock, paper, scissors
objectives: random.randint(a, b) gives a random integer, including both ends
input() returns a string, so int() converts it before comparing numbers
A for loop with range limits the number of guesses, and break leaves early on a right guess
Rock, paper, scissors uses an outer game loop, an inner loop that repeats until the input is valid, and counters for wins, losses and ties

items.heading: Creating functions with def
objectives: def defines a function; its code runs when the function is called, not when it's defined
A call is the function's name followed by parentheses; afterwards execution goes back to the line that called it
Functions remove duplicated code, so programs are shorter and easier to update

items.heading: Arguments and parameters
objectives: Parameters are the variables in the definition; arguments are the values passed in a call
The terms define, call, pass, argument and parameter
Parameters are local: they're forgotten when the function returns, and using one outside it causes a NameError

items.heading: Return values and return statements
objectives: return gives the value that the call evaluates to
A call can be used inside an expression, including as an argument to another call

items.heading: The None value
objectives: None means the absence of a value; it's the only value of the NoneType type, and is capitalized
print() returns None
A function without a return statement, or with a bare return, returns None

items.heading: Named parameters
objectives: Keyword arguments are identified by name, not position
print()'s end= replaces the newline at the end, and sep= replaces the space between arguments

items.heading: The call stack
objectives: Each call adds a frame to the call stack that remembers where to return; returning removes it
The stack is last in, first out
When the stack is empty, execution is outside all functions

items.heading: Local and global scopes: the scope rules
objectives: Variables assigned in a function are local to that call; there's one global scope and a new local scope for each call
Global code can't use local variables
One function can't use another function's local variables
Local code can read global variables
The same name can be different variables in different scopes
A local scope and its variables are destroyed when the call returns

items.heading: The global statement, and working out a variable's scope
objectives: global name at the start of a function makes assignments change the global variable
The rules: outside all functions it's global; with a global statement it's global; assigned in the function it's local; only read there, it's global
Using a local variable before assigning it raises UnboundLocalError instead of falling back to the global one

items.heading: Exception handling with try and except
objectives: Code that might fail goes in try; the handling code goes in except, such as except ZeroDivisionError:
When an error happens, the rest of the try block is skipped and except runs; otherwise except is skipped
Errors raised inside functions called from the try block are caught too
int() on text that isn't a number raises ValueError, which except ValueError: catches

items.heading: Short programs: Zigzag and Spike
objectives: time.sleep() pauses a program, and while True: runs until it's stopped
Catching KeyboardInterrupt lets Ctrl-C end the program cleanly with sys.exit()
String replication and range() with a negative step make the patterns

items.heading: Raising exceptions with raise
objectives: raise Exception('message') stops normal execution and jumps to an except clause
Without a try and except around it, the program crashes and shows the message; usually a function raises and its caller handles it
except Exception as err: stores the exception in a variable, and str(err) gives its message

items.heading: Assertions with assert
objectives: An assert statement raises AssertionError when its condition is False
Assertions are sanity checks for programmer mistakes: don't catch them, let the program fail fast
Use exceptions, not assertions, for expected problems such as bad user input or a missing file

items.heading: Logging with the logging module, including logging levels
objectives: Setup: import logging, then logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format=...)
Five levels from lowest to highest: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL, each with its own function such as logging.debug()
basicConfig's level hides messages below it; logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL) turns all messages off
basicConfig(filename=...) writes the log to a file
Logging is for the programmer and easy to switch off; print() is for the user

items.heading: Using the debugger: stepping through code and setting breakpoints
objectives: The debugger runs a program one line at a time and shows the variables' values
Step Over runs the next line, running any function it calls at full speed; Step In goes into the function; Step Out finishes the current function
Continue runs normally until the program ends or reaches a breakpoint
A breakpoint, set by clicking a line number in Mu, pauses execution at that line

items.heading: The list data type: indexes and negative indexes
objectives: A list is an ordered sequence in square brackets, and [] is the empty list
Indexes start at 0; an index past the end raises IndexError, and a float index raises TypeError
Negative indexes count from the end: index -1 is the last item
Lists can contain lists, reached with two indexes one after the other

items.heading: Slices and the len() function
objectives: A slice such as items[1:4] gives a new list of the items at 1, 2 and 3; the end index isn't included
Leaving out the start or end means from the beginning or to the end, so [:] copies the whole list
len() gives the number of items

items.heading: Changing values, concatenation, replication and del
objectives: Assigning to an index changes that item
+ joins lists and * repeats one
del with an index removes an item, and the items after it move down

items.heading: for loops with lists
objectives: for item in items loops over the items
for i in range(len(items)) loops over the indexes when you need them

items.heading: The in and not in operators
objectives: in and not in check whether a value is in a list and give True or False

items.heading: The multiple assignment trick
objectives: a, b, c = items unpacks a three-item list into variables in one line
The number of variables must match the number of items, or Python raises ValueError

items.heading: Enumerating list items
objectives: enumerate() gives the index and the item on each pass: for index, item in enumerate(items)

items.heading: Random selection and ordering
objectives: random.choice() returns one random item from a list
random.shuffle() reorders a list in place and doesn't return a new list

items.heading: Augmented assignment operators
objectives: x += 1 is short for x = x + 1; there are also -=, *=, /= and %=
+= and *= also work on strings and lists

items.heading: List methods for finding, adding, removing, sorting and reversing values
objectives: index() returns the first position of a value, and raises ValueError if it's missing
append() adds to the end; insert(i, value) adds at a position
remove() deletes the first matching value, and raises ValueError if it's missing
sort() sorts in place, with reverse=True for descending and key=str.lower to ignore case; it can't sort a mix of numbers and strings
These methods change the list in place and return None, so assigning a list to the result of its own sort() loses the list
reverse() reverses a list in place

items.heading: Short-circuiting Boolean operators
objectives: and doesn't evaluate its right side when the left side is False; or doesn't when the left side is True (short-circuiting)
This makes it safe to check a list's length and then index it in the same condition

items.heading: Mutable and immutable data types
objectives: Lists are mutable; strings and tuples are immutable, and assigning to a character of a string raises TypeError
To change a string, build a new one from slices and concatenation
Reassigning a variable replaces its value, while methods like append() modify the list itself

items.heading: The tuple data type, and converting with list() and tuple()
objectives: Tuples use parentheses and can't be changed
A one-item tuple needs a trailing comma; without it the parentheses just group a value
list() and tuple() convert between them, and list() on a string gives a list of its characters

items.heading: References: passing lists to functions, copy() and deepcopy()
objectives: Variables hold references to lists, so assigning a list to another variable doesn't copy it
A function that changes a list passed to it changes the caller's list
copy.copy() makes a separate copy; copy.deepcopy() also copies the lists inside a list

items.heading: Short programs: a Magic 8 Ball with a list, and a Matrix-style screensaver
objectives: Short programs that pick items from a list at random and print them in a loop

items.heading: Dictionary basics: keys, values and key-value pairs
objectives: A dictionary maps keys to values inside curly braces
Keys can be many types, not just integers, and don't need to start at 0
d[key] gets a value; a key that isn't there raises KeyError

items.heading: Dictionaries compared with lists
objectives: Two dictionaries with the same key-value pairs are equal, whatever the order
Dictionaries can't be sliced like lists
Lists are reached by integer position; dictionaries by key

items.heading: The in and not in operators with dictionaries
objectives: key in d checks the keys, the same as key in d.keys()
value in d.values() checks the values

items.heading: The keys(), values() and items() methods
objectives: keys(), values() and items() give list-like values you can loop over but not change
list(d.keys()) makes a real list
for k, v in d.items(): unpacks each key-value pair

items.heading: The get() method
objectives: get(key, fallback) returns the fallback instead of raising KeyError when the key is missing

items.heading: The setdefault() method
objectives: setdefault(key, value) sets the value only if the key is missing, and returns the key's value either way
Counting characters: setdefault(character, 0), then add 1
pprint.pprint() prints a dictionary in a readable layout

items.heading: Project: an interactive chessboard simulator
objectives: The board is a dictionary with square names as keys and short strings naming each piece's color and type as values
Moving a piece copies the value to the new square and deletes the old key
Data structures model real things; this program doesn't enforce the rules of chess

items.heading: Nested dictionaries and lists
objectives: Dictionaries and lists can contain each other
Nested data is read with nested loops or items()

items.heading: String literals and quotes
objectives: Strings can use single or double quotes; double quotes let a string contain a single quote without escaping

items.heading: Escape characters
objectives: A backslash starts an escape character: \' and \" for quotes, \n for a newline, \t for a tab, \\ for a backslash

items.heading: Raw strings
objectives: An r before the opening quote makes a raw string, where backslashes are kept as they are; handy for Windows paths

items.heading: Multiline strings
objectives: Triple quotes make a string that spans several lines, newlines included
Triple-quoted strings are also used as multiline comments

items.heading: Indexing and slicing strings
objectives: Strings are indexed and sliced like lists, including negative indexes
Slicing doesn't change the original string

items.heading: The in and not in operators with strings
objectives: in and not in check for a substring, and the check is case-sensitive

items.heading: f-strings
objectives: f-strings put expressions in braces: f'My name is {name}'
{{ and }} give literal braces
Older styles still seen: '%s' % value and the format() method

items.heading: String methods for case and validation
objectives: upper() and lower() return new strings and leave the original unchanged
isupper() and islower() need at least one letter to be True
isalpha(), isalnum(), isdecimal(), isspace() and istitle() check what a string contains, which helps validate input
String methods can be chained, each working on the result of the one before

items.heading: startswith() and endswith()
objectives: startswith() and endswith() check how a string begins and ends

items.heading: join() and split()
objectives: join() is called on the separator string and takes a list of strings
split() splits on whitespace by default, or on a separator such as '\n'

items.heading: Justifying text with rjust(), ljust() and center()
objectives: rjust(), ljust() and center() pad a string to a width, with an optional fill character

items.heading: Removing whitespace with strip(), lstrip() and rstrip()
objectives: strip() removes whitespace from both ends, lstrip() and rstrip() from one end
An argument gives the characters to remove from the ends instead

items.heading: ord() and chr()
objectives: ord('A') is 65 and chr(65) is 'A': every character has a number code

items.heading: Copying and pasting with the pyperclip module
objectives: pyperclip.copy() and pyperclip.paste() use the clipboard; the module is installed separately

items.heading: Projects: adding bullets to wiki markup, and a Pig Latin translator
objectives: Transforming clipboard text line by line: split on newlines, change each line in a loop, join and copy back
Transforming words letter by letter while keeping punctuation and capitalization

items.heading: Text Pattern Matching with Regular Expressions
Files and file paths
objectives: Windows separates folders with backslashes; macOS and Linux use forward slashes
pathlib's Path objects work on every system, and forward slashes are the best practice

items.heading: The pathlib module
objectives: from pathlib import Path; parts of a path are joined with the / operator
One of the first two values joined with / must be a Path object; joining two plain strings with / is an error
Path.home() is the user's home folder

items.heading: The current working directory
objectives: Path.cwd() (or os.getcwd()) gives the current working directory, and os.chdir() changes it
Paths that don't start at the root folder are relative to the working directory

items.heading: Absolute and relative paths
objectives: An absolute path starts at the root folder; a relative path is relative to the working directory
. means this folder and .. the parent folder
is_absolute() checks a path, and Path.cwd() / a relative path or absolute() makes it absolute

items.heading: Creating new folders
objectives: os.makedirs() creates every missing folder in a path
Path.mkdir() creates one folder, and mkdir(parents=True) creates missing parents too

items.heading: Getting file and folder details
objectives: A path's parts: anchor, parent, name, stem and suffix (and drive on Windows), plus the parts tuple
The parent is the directory name and the name is the base name
stat().st_size gives the size in bytes, and st_mtime the last-modified time

items.heading: Finding files with glob patterns
objectives: Glob patterns: * matches any text and ? one character, as in p.glob('*.txt')
glob() returns a generator, so loop over it or wrap it in list()

items.heading: Checking whether files and folders exist
objectives: exists(), is_file() and is_dir() check what a path points to

items.heading: Opening files with open()
objectives: open() returns a file object; its modes are 'r' (read, the default), 'w' (write) and 'a' (append)
Pass encoding='utf-8' when opening text files

items.heading: Reading file contents
objectives: read() returns the whole file as one string; readlines() returns a list of lines, each ending in \n
Path.read_text() reads a text file in one call

items.heading: Writing to files
objectives: Write mode overwrites an existing file and append mode adds to its end; both create the file if it's missing
write() doesn't add a newline the way print() does
Path.write_text() writes a file in one call and returns the number of characters written

items.heading: Closing files, and the with statement
objectives: Every opened file should be closed
with open(...) as f: closes the file automatically when the block ends

items.heading: Saving variables with the shelve module
objectives: shelve.open() saves variables in binary files that work like a dictionary
A shelf can be read and written once it's open; list() turns its keys() and values() into lists

items.heading: Project: generating random quiz files
objectives: The project combines a dictionary, random.shuffle() and random.sample(), and writes many files in a loop
